facts.claim: The CHP can obtain copies only of collision reports that the CHP itself investigates.
facts.quote: No. The CHP can only obtain copies of collision reports we investigate.

facts.claim: Vehicle Code 20012 says required accident reports and supplemental reports are for the confidential use of the DMV and the CHP.
facts.quote: shall be for the confidential use of the Department of Motor Vehicles and the Department of the California Highway Patrol

facts.claim: Vehicle Code 20008 requires every police department to forward to the CHP's main office in Sacramento the reports (or copies) it received during the previous calendar month of accidents it is responsible for investigating.
facts.quote: every police department which received a report during the previous calendar month of an accident which it is responsible for investigating shall forward the report or a copy thereof to the main office of the Department of the California Highway Patrol at Sacramento

facts.claim: The CHP's Crash Investigation Manual (revised August 2025) says all crash investigation reports are to be sent to the CHP to collect traffic safety data used by local, state and federal entities.
facts.quote: All crash investigation reports shall be transmitted in a timely manner to the CHP for the collection of traffic safety data used by local, state, and federal entities.

facts.claim: A proper Party of Interest can request a copy of a CHP crash report online through the Crash Portal, without going to the CHP Area office where the report was filed.
facts.quote: may request a copy of a CHP crash report/investigation, without having to go to the CHP Area office where the crash report was filed online through the Crash Portal.

facts.claim: A CHP Area office page (Dublin) tells people they can visit the CHP Crash report portal to get a copy of a CHP-investigated crash report.
facts.quote: Visit the CHP Crash report portal

facts.claim: A proper Party of Interest can also request a CHP crash report in person or by mail at the nearest CHP Area office by completing form CHP 190.
facts.quote: A proper Party of Interest may also submit a request for a copy of a CHP crash report/investigation in person or via mail to the nearest CHP Area office by completing a CHP 190

facts.claim: The CHP 190 form posted on the CHP website is marked CHP 190 (Rev. 11-03) OPI 008.
To get a report by mail, you can complete form CHP 190 (Application for Release of Information) or simply write a personal letter.
facts.quote: Follow the procedures below to obtain a copy of the collision report through the mail by completing a form CHP 190 (Application for Release of Information) available on this web site, or you may simply write a personal letter.

facts.claim: Send the completed form or letter to the CHP office that reported the collision, with verification that you are a proper Party of Interest.
facts.quote: Send the completed form or personal letter to the CHP office that reported the collision, along with verification that you are a proper Party of Interest.

facts.claim: After the CHP verifies that you are a proper party of interest, it mails a copy of the report to your address once it receives payment.
facts.quote: Once the CHP has your request and verified you are a proper party of interest, a copy of the report will be mailed to your address upon receipt of payment.

facts.claim: A Party of Interest can go to any CHP office and pay a nominal fee for a copy of a CHP-investigated report.
facts.quote: If you are a Party of Interest, you can go to any CHP office and pay a nominal fee for a copy of the report.

facts.claim: Any CHP office can get a copy of a CHP collision report or arrange for one to be mailed to your address.
facts.quote: Any CHP office will be able to get a copy of a CHP collision report or arrange for one to be mailed to your address.

facts.claim: CHP General Order 110.2 says a person with proper interest can get a copy of a CHP-generated collision report from any CHP Area in the state, regardless of the CHP jurisdiction where the collision happened.
facts.quote: A person who has proper interest can obtain a copy of a California Highway Patrol (CHP) generated collision report from any CHP Area in the state, regardless of the CHP jurisdiction in which the collision occurred.

facts.claim: Traffic collision reports can be picked up at any CHP office during normal business hours.
facts.quote: Traffic Collision Reports are available to be picked up at any CHP office during normal business hours.

facts.claim: The CHP says you can have your insurance provider obtain a copy of the collision report and give you a copy, which may save you the report fee.
facts.quote: Have your insurance provider obtain a copy of the collision report and give you a copy (this may save you the report fee).

facts.claim: CHP General Order 110.2 lists sending a copy by e-mail from a CHP Area to an e-mail address requested by the person with proper interest as one way to provide a report.
facts.quote: or sending a copy via e-mail from one CHP Area to an e-mail address requested by the person who has proper interest.

facts.claim: On the CHP 190, give the crash date, or an approximate date if you do not know the exact date.
facts.quote: If you do not know the exact date, provide an approximate date.

facts.claim: On the CHP 190, give the crash location, listing as much information as possible if you do not know the exact location.
facts.quote: If you do not know the exact location, list as much information as possible.

facts.claim: On the CHP 190, list the driver or owner of the vehicle, or your own name and address if only your property was damaged.
facts.quote: List the driver or owner of the vehicle. If only your property was damaged, please list your name and address.

facts.claim: Attach a photocopy of your driver license or picture ID card to the request; if you have neither, the CHP 190 must be certified by a notary.
facts.quote: Photocopy your driver license or picture identification card and attach it to your request for a collision report. If you do not have either of these forms of identification, then, the CHP 190 form must be certified by a notary.

facts.claim: The applicant signs the CHP 190 declaring under penalty of perjury that they are the party of interest checked on the form.
facts.quote: I DECLARE UNDER PENALTY OF PERJURY THAT I AM THE PARTY OF INTEREST

facts.claim: On the CHP 190, an insurance company or adjusting agency representative must have been a carrier for an involved party at the time of the accident and must present a policy or claim number.
facts.quote: Must have been a carrier for involved party at time of accident. Policy or claim number must be presented.

facts.claim: If you know the report number, the CHP asks you to put it on your check.
facts.quote: Please place the report number on your check, if you know it.

facts.claim: The CHP's posted charge for a collision report of 01-25 pages is $10.00.
The CHP's posted charge for a collision report of 26-50 pages is $20.00.
The CHP's posted charge for a collision report of 51-75 pages is $30.00.
The CHP's posted charge for a collision report of 76-100 pages is $40.00.
For reports over 100 pages, the CHP charges $10.00 for each additional 25 pages or portion thereof.
facts.quote: $10.00 — Over 100 - for each additional 25 pages or portion thereof

facts.claim: The CHP adds no extra charge for handling or mailing.
facts.quote: There is no extra charge for handling or mailing.

facts.claim: A personal check or money order made out to the California Highway Patrol must be sent with your request.
facts.quote: Your personal check or money order must be sent with your request and made out to the California Highway Patrol.

facts.claim: The CHP does not accept cash for mailed requests and says it does not accept credit or debit cards at this time.
facts.quote: NO CASH PLEASE if you are requesting the report by mail. We do not accept Credit or Debit cards at this time.

facts.claim: The CHP FAQ says the collision report fee is paid by cash or check and tells you to contact your local Area office about it.
facts.quote: There is a fee for the collision report (cash or check); contact your local area office.

facts.claim: The CHP says it charges a nominal fee to cover reproduction costs and tells you to contact the CHP office where the report was filed to find the cost of your report.
facts.quote: The CHP charges only a nominal fee to cover reproduction costs (To determine the cost of your report, please contact the CHP office where the report was filed).

facts.claim: The CHP tells CHP 190 filers to contact the Area office they are submitting the form to for the exact fee.
facts.quote: Submit applicable fees (contact the Area office you will be submitting the form to for the exact amount).

facts.claim: CHP General Order 110.2 (revised December 2014) sets a charge of $10.00 per 25 pages for report copies in any format.
facts.quote: Report copies provided in any format, require a charge of $10.00 per 25 pages.

facts.claim: CHP General Order 110.2 says a person with proper interest may review a report in its entirety without charge.
facts.quote: A person who has proper interest may review a report in its entirety without charge.

facts.claim: Under Vehicle Code 20012, a request for a copy of an accident report must be accompanied by a fee that may not exceed the actual cost of providing the copy.
facts.quote: A request for a copy of an accident report shall be accompanied by payment of a fee, provided such fee shall not exceed the actual cost of providing the copy.

facts.claim: The CHP advises calling the CHP office handling the incident ahead of time to see whether your report is available for pick up.
facts.quote: Call the CHP office overseeing the incident ahead of time to see if your traffic collision report is available for pick up.

facts.claim: The CHP lists proper Parties of Interest as drivers, bicyclists, pedestrians, passengers, parents of minors, legal guardians, vehicle or property owners, legal representatives, manufacturer representatives, and insurance companies with a valid claim or policy number.
facts.quote: A proper Party of Interest (i.e., Drivers, Bicyclists, Pedestrians, Passengers, Parents of Minors, Legal Guardians, Vehicle or Property Owners, Legal representatives, Manufacturer Representatives, or Insurance Companies with a valid claim or policy number)

facts.claim: The CHP says any involved or interested party can get a copy of a collision report.
facts.quote: Any involved or interested party can get a copy of a collision report.

facts.claim: The CHP FAQ says that to receive a copy you must be an involved party, passenger, property owner, or licensed insurance agent with a signed release from an involved party.
facts.quote: To receive a copy of a report you must be an involved party, passenger, property owner, or licensed insurance agent (with a signed release from your insured, an involved party).

facts.claim: If you are not sure you are entitled to a copy, the CHP asks you to contact any CHP Area office to verify whether you are a proper Party of Interest.
facts.quote: If you are not sure you are entitled to a copy of the report/investigation, please contact any CHP Area office to verify whether you are a proper Party of Interest.

facts.claim: Under Vehicle Code 20012, reports are disclosed to any person with a proper interest, including the drivers involved, their guardians or conservators, the parent of a minor driver, a driver's authorized representative, and any named injured person.
facts.quote: to any person who may have a proper interest therein, including, but not limited to, the driver or drivers involved, or the guardian or conservator thereof, the parent of a minor driver, the authorized representative of a driver, or to any named person injured therein

facts.claim: Vehicle Code 20012 also covers owners of damaged vehicles or property, persons who may incur civil liability, and attorneys who declare under penalty of perjury that they represent any of those persons.
facts.quote: the owners of vehicles or property damaged thereby, persons who may incur civil liability, including liability based upon a breach of warranty arising out of the accident, and any attorney who declares under penalty of perjury that he or she represents any of the above persons

facts.claim: Under CHP General Order 110.2, parents of adult children are not persons of proper interest unless they have a signed authorization from the involved adult child.
facts.quote: Parents of adult children are not considered a person of proper interest, unless they have a signed authorization from the involved adult child.

facts.claim: For fatal collisions, CHP General Order 110.2 places proper interest with the surviving spouse, minor children through their guardians, or a court-appointed family member under Probate Code 6401.
facts.quote: In cases involving fatal collisions; proper interest lies with the surviving spouse, minor children when released through their guardians, or court appointed family member per California Probate Code 6401.

facts.claim: CHP General Order 110.2 authorizes insurance company representatives who supply the policy or claim number in effect at the time of the collision and hold the name of the insured.
facts.quote: Representatives of insurance companies that supply the policy or claim number that was in effect at the time of the collision and hold the name of the insured.

facts.claim: Under CHP General Order 110.2, a declaration under penalty of perjury that someone represents a person with proper interest permits release of the report to the attorney or their identified agent.
facts.quote: Such declarations permit release of the report to the attorney or their identified agent.

facts.claim: Vehicle or component manufacturer representatives must present a letter from the manufacturer, dated within the last 12 months, certifying their authority.
facts.quote: Such representatives must present a letter from the manufacturer, dated within the last 12 months, certifying their authority.

facts.claim: Under CHP General Order 110.2, until a collision report is complete the CHP can give the public only the time, date and location of the collision, the make of the vehicles, and occupant names (except in fatal collisions).
facts.quote: Until a collision report is complete, the following information can be provided to the public: (1) Time of collision. (2) Date of collision. (3) Location of collision. (4) Make of vehicle(s) involved. (5) Names of vehicle occupants (other than fatal collisions).

facts.claim: If you do not know which police department investigated the collision, the CHP says to contact your local police department or a CHP office for help identifying the right law enforcement agency.
facts.quote: If you do not know the police department who investigated the collision, you can either contact your local police department or CHP Office to assist you in identifying the proper law enforcement agency.

facts.claim: Vehicle Code 20012 makes the law enforcement agency to which an accident was reported, as well as the CHP, responsible for disclosing the entire contents of its accident reports.
facts.quote: the Department of the California Highway Patrol or the law enforcement agency to whom the accident was reported shall disclose the entire contents of the reports

facts.claim: The CHP's Crash Investigation Manual says allied agencies should establish crash report retention schedules suited to their needs.
facts.quote: Allied agencies should establish a retention schedule suited to their needs.

facts.claim: You or your insurance agent, broker or legal representative must send an SR-1 report to the DMV within 10 days if anyone is injured (however minor) or killed, or property damage is over $1000.
facts.quote: You or your insurance agent, broker, or legal representative must complete an SR-1 report and send it to DMV within 10 days if someone is injured (no matter how minor the injury) or killed, or property damage is over $1000.

facts.claim: The DMV says an SR-1 is required in addition to any report made to the police, the CHP or your insurance company.
facts.quote: An SR-1 report is required in addition to any other report made to the police, CHP, or your insurance company.

facts.claim: The DMV says paper SR-1 submissions are likely to take longer to process.
facts.quote: Please note that paper submissions are likely to take longer to process.

facts.claim: Vehicle Code 16000 requires an accident that caused more than $1,000 in damage to any one person's property, or bodily injury, or death, to be reported within 10 days after the accident.
facts.quote: that has resulted in damage to the property of any one person in excess of one thousand dollars ($1,000), or in bodily injury, or in the death of any person shall report the accident, within 10 days after the accident

facts.claim: Under Vehicle Code 16000, no SR-1 report is required if the vehicle was owned or leased by, or under the direction of, the United States, California, another state, or a local agency.
facts.quote: A report is not required under subdivision (a) if the motor vehicle involved in the accident was owned or leased by, or under the direction of, the United States, this state, another state, or a local agency.

facts.claim: The SR-1 form (Rev. 6/2025) says California law requires accidents on a California street/highway or private property to be reported to the DMV within 10 days if there was an injury, death or property damage over $1,000.
facts.quote: California law requires traffic accidents on a California street/highway or private property to be reported to the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) within 10 days if there was an injury, death or property damage in excess of $1,000.

facts.claim: The SR-1 form says the driver must file it with the DMV regardless of fault.
facts.quote: The law requires the driver to file this SR 1 form with DMV regardless of fault.

facts.claim: The SR-1 form says reports filed with a law enforcement agency, insurance company or the CHP do not satisfy the SR-1 filing requirement.
facts.quote: This report must be made in addition to any other report filed with a law enforcement agency, insurance company, or the California Highway Patrol (CHP) as their reports do not satisfy the filing requirement.

facts.claim: The SR-1 form warns that late reporting could lead the DMV to suspend a driver license.
facts.quote: Untimely reporting could result in DMV suspending a driver license.

facts.claim: An insurance agent, attorney or other designated representative may file the SR-1 for the driver.
facts.quote: An insurance agent, attorney, or other designated representative may file the report for the driver.

facts.claim: A paper SR-1 is mailed to the DMV Insurance Unit, Mail Station J237, P.O. Box 942884, Sacramento, CA 94284-0884.
facts.quote: Department of Motor Vehicles Insurance Unit Mail Station J237 P.O. Box 942884 Sacramento, CA 94284-0884

facts.claim: Under Vehicle Code 20008, if the accident occurred within a city, that written report may go to either the CHP or the city's police department.
facts.quote: if the accident occurred within a city, to either the Department of the California Highway Patrol or the police department of the city in which the accident occurred

facts.claim: The CHP says it cannot accept traffic collision reports online at this time.
facts.quote: At this time, we are unable to accept reports online.

facts.claim: You can file a traffic collision report at any CHP office in California, wherever the collision occurred.
facts.quote: You may visit any CHP office anywhere in California to file a traffic collision report, regardless of where the collision occurred.

facts.claim: CHP General Order 110.2 says the authority for releasing collision reports is California Vehicle Code Section 20012.
facts.quote: The authority for release of collision reports is contained in California Vehicle Code (VC) Section 20012.

facts.claim: CHP officers normally give parties of interest at a crash scene a CHP 418, Crash Report Information, form that tells them the Traffic Crash Report will be available.
facts.quote: The CHP 418 shall normally be used by the CHP to notify parties of interest at a crash scene of the availability of the Traffic Crash Report.

facts.claim: The CHP's Crash Investigation Manual says all crash reports shall be retained for a minimum of four years from the date of the crash.
facts.quote: All crash reports shall be retained for a minimum of four years from the date of the crash.

facts.claim: The California Crash Reporting System (CCRS) dataset on data.ca.gov is described as statistic crash records within the State of California.
facts.quote: Statistic crash records within State of California

facts.claim: For a mailed request, the CHP FAQ says to include a copy of your CHP 418 (Crash Report Information) card and a copy of your valid driver license.
facts.quote: Remember to include a copy of your CHP 418 (Crash Report Information) card and a copy of your valid driver license.

facts.claim: The CHP says the CHP 190 form is available in both English and Spanish.
facts.quote: The form contains areas to fill out information and is available in both English and Spanish.

facts.claim: To request by mail, mail the CHP 190 and a photocopy of your driver license to the CHP office (jurisdiction) that filed the report.
facts.quote: If you prefer to handle this through the mail, you can complete the form CHP 190 (Application for Release of Information), which can be downloaded from this website. Mail the form and a photocopy of your driver license to the CHP jurisdiction that filed the report

facts.claim: People who live outside California can get a CHP collision report by mail.
facts.quote: How can I get a copy of a CHP collision report if I live out-of-state? You can obtain a copy of a collision report by mail.

facts.claim: The statewide CHP FAQ also points people to the CHP Crash Report Search website to get their crash report.
facts.quote: You can also visit the following website to obtain your crash report: CHP | Crash Report Search

facts.claim: Under CHP General Order 110.2, a CHP Area can fax a copy of the report to another CHP Area or to any other location the person with proper interest asks for.
facts.quote: Sending a fax copy of the report from one CHP Area to another CHP Area, or any other location requested by person who has proper interest.

facts.claim: The CHP lists insurance companies, attorneys, the coroner, Caltrans and parents of minors as examples of interested parties who can get a collision report.
facts.quote: Interested parties include but are not limited to: Insurance companies Attorneys Coroner Caltrans Parents of minors

facts.claim: Under CHP General Order 110.2, when one collision is a primary or associated cause of later collisions, all drivers and passengers in all of those reports have proper interest.
facts.quote: When a collision is either a primary or associated collision factor of a subsequent collision or collisions, all drivers and passengers in all reports are considered to be persons who have proper interest.

facts.claim: CHP General Order 110.2 also authorizes any person, company or corporation named in a legal action, or who may incur civil liability from a collision, to buy a copy of the report.
facts.quote: Any person, company, or corporation named in a legal action or who may incur civil liability resulting from a collision.

facts.claim: Under CHP General Order 110.2, a written statement saying you represent a person with proper interest counts as a declaration under penalty of perjury.
facts.quote: A written statement from an individual stating they represent a person who has proper interest is deemed to be a declaration under penalty of perjury.

facts.claim: A person requesting a report as someone's representative must complete a CHP 190 before buying the report.
facts.quote: The individual shall complete a CHP 190, Application for Release of Information, (Annex A) prior to purchasing the report.

facts.claim: Manufacturer representatives are parties of interest only for collisions involving the manufacturer's make of vehicle, or vehicles with its component installed.
facts.quote: Such representatives are parties of interest for only those collisions which involved the manufacturer's make of vehicle or vehicle(s) in which a component has been installed.

facts.claim: On request, the CHP Area commander schedules a discussion of the collision investigation between a person with proper interest (or their agent) and the officer who wrote the report.
facts.quote: Upon request, the CHP Area commander shall schedule discussions of collision investigations between a person who has proper interest, or agents thereof, and officer who wrote the report.

facts.claim: A person with proper interest may not record a case discussion with the CHP officer.
facts.quote: A person who has proper interest shall not be allowed to record these discussions.

facts.claim: An involved party who disagrees with part of a CHP collision report can write a supplemental statement that includes the report number, their name and the items they dispute.
facts.quote: If you are the involved party in a traffic collision, and disagree with any portion of the report, you may write a "supplemental" statement. In your written statement, please include: The report number Your name The specific item or items with which you disagree

facts.claim: The supplemental statement can be taken to any CHP office or sent by US Mail, and the CHP replies by US Mail.
facts.quote: You may bring this statement into any CHP office, or send it via US Mail. You will receive a response by US Mail.

facts.claim: Caltrans keeps copies of all state highway-related crash reports for ten years from the month of the crash, and requests go to the Caltrans Legal Division (for duplicates missing from local files or purged).
facts.quote: The California Department of Transportation retains copies of all state highway-related reports for ten years from the month of the crash. Requests should be directed to the Caltrans Legal Division.

facts.claim: CHP Headquarters keeps copies of fatal crash reports for the current year plus three.
facts.quote: California Highway Patrol Headquarters retains copies of fatal crashes for the current year plus three.

facts.claim: The CHP keeps reports of crashes involving felony charges for serious bodily injury or death for seven years from the crash date.
facts.quote: Reports for crashes involving felony charges for serious bodily injury or death shall be retained for seven years from the date of the crash.

facts.claim: The CHP keeps unsolved fatal hit-and-run crash investigations indefinitely.
facts.quote: All unsolved fatal hit-and-run crash investigations shall be retained indefinitely.

facts.claim: Under Vehicle Code 20008, if the agency that receives a driver's injury or fatal accident report is not responsible for investigating it, that agency must immediately forward the report to the responsible law enforcement agency.
facts.quote: If the agency which receives the report is not responsible for investigating the accident, it shall immediately forward the report to the law enforcement agency which is responsible for investigating the accident.

facts.claim: Under Vehicle Code 20008(b), the owner or driver of a common carrier vehicle in an injury or fatal accident reports to the CHP by the 10th day of the month after the accident.
facts.quote: The owner or driver of a common carrier vehicle involved in any such accident shall make a like report to the Department of California Highway Patrol on or before the 10th day of the month following the accident.

facts.claim: The DMV does not accept an SR-1, or act against non-reporting or uninsured motorists, unless someone involved (or their designee) sends the SR-1 and the DMV receives it within one calendar year of the accident.
facts.quote: DMV does not accept reports or take actions against non-reporting or uninsured motorists unless this SR 1 form is sent to DMV by someone involved in the accident or their designee and the report is received by DMV within one calendar year of the accident date.

facts.claim: The SR-1 form says accidents on a military base, or on the driver's own property involving only the driver's personal property with no injury or death, are not reportable.
facts.quote: occurring on a military base or occurring on the driver's own property involving only the personal property of the driver and there was no injury or death are not reportable.

facts.claim: The DMV lets drivers file an SR-1 online with its 'Start an SR-1' button.
facts.quote: Report a traffic accident by filing an SR-1. Start an SR-1

facts.claim: Before filing an SR-1, the DMV says to gather your DL/ID card, your license plate number or VIN, your insurance information, and the other party's vehicle and insurance information if applicable.
facts.quote: Your driver’s license or identification (DL/ID) card Your vehicle’s license plate number or vehicle identification number (VIN) Your vehicle’s insurance information Other party’s vehicle and insurance information, if applicable

facts.claim: The DMV offers a Spanish version of the SR-1 form as a PDF.
facts.quote: A printable copy of the form (PDF) is available if needed. Please note that paper submissions are likely to take longer to process. Spanish version (PDF).

gaps.reason: I could not confirm the CHP Crash Portal's price or any card or convenience fee. crashes.chp.ca.gov refused connections from both WebFetch and the fallback fetcher, and no chp.ca.gov page I read gives a portal fee. Non-official sources disagree: some say $22 and some say free. Neither figure should be published until someone confirms it on the portal.

The CHP's FAQ pages post a page-based fee schedule ($10.00 per 01-25 pages and so on). But the Request a Crash Report page and the CHP 190 page both tell requesters to contact the Area office for the exact amount. The guide should present the schedule as CHP's posted rates and advise confirming with the office. For in-person payment, the only stated methods are 'cash or check' (FAQ). For mail, cards are explicitly not accepted.

No official page I could open says how soon after a crash a CHP report is usually available. A search-engine snippet credited to the Crash Portal's registration page says reports are 'typically available within eight (8) business days', and news articles repeat this. I could not open the portal to confirm it. The CHP FAQ only says to call the office ahead of time.

I could not confirm what the Crash Portal requires because the portal would not load. Unconfirmed points include account registration, crash card or QR code details, accepted payment methods and whether downloads are immediate. Official CHP pages only link to its login page.
No official CHP page I read names a third-party vendor portal, such as LexisNexis BuyCrash or CARFAX Crashdocs, for CHP reports.

I did not research how individual city police departments and county sheriffs handle requests, what they charge, or which vendor portals they use. I found no statewide official directory of them. Only the general Vehicle Code 20012 rules apply statewide: disclosure to people with a proper interest, and a fee no higher than the actual cost.

gaps.reason: No official online portal for first-party PD-10 requests was found. MPD's page lists only email, mail and in-person (by appointment). No DC government page found names or links a vendor crash-report portal such as BuyCrash or Crashdocs. The only online portal found is the DC FOIA public access website, which is the third-party (FOIA) route.

The PD-10 email address on the MPD page is hidden by Cloudflare email protection in the page source, so text fetchers see '[email protected]'. I decoded it from the page's data-cfemail attribute as mpd.public-docs@dc.gov, which is what a browser shows. The quote for that fact is the browser-rendered sentence. Check it in a browser before publishing.

No official source says how soon after a crash a PD-10 becomes available to request. The only time frames found are the six-week mail-in processing time and the DC FOIA response deadlines. MPD training material says officers must submit and approve reports by the end of their tour, but that is not a statement about public availability.

MPD's page gives the $3 insurer fee but not the payment method, payee or any card or convenience fee. The page also says PD-10 requests are first-party only while describing insurer copies, and it doesn't explain how insurers request them. MPD's FOIA page says FOIA processing fees may be charged but gives no amounts.

The header of PD Form 10B still shows an older address (MPD Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) Office, 300 Indiana Avenue, NW, Room 4153), and its footer is dated January 14, 2015 (GO-SPT-401.03 Attachment B). The current request page says to mail requests to the Public Documents Section at 441 4th Street, NW, Room 550 South. The guide should use the page's address, not the form header.

DC has no separate county or city crash-report system beyond MPD, and no DC government page was found that says what to do when another police agency operating in DC handled the crash (for example U.S. Park Police, U.S. Capitol Police or Metro Transit Police), or whether MPD holds those reports. MPD's page covers only reports written by MPD officers. Lead only, not recorded as a fact: the U.S. Park Police's own federal pages say crash reports for its Washington, D.C.-area incidents are requested from USPP Records (https://www.nps.gov/aboutus/foia/how-to-request-an-accident-report.htm, and https://www.nps.gov/subjects/uspp/foia-requests.htm, which gives USPP_Records@nps.gov). These are federal nps.gov pages, outside this task's state/DC source definition.

No official source says outright whether MPD's Public Documents Section holds crash reports from every law-enforcement agency in DC or only its own. Its page describes only MPD officers' PD-10 and PD-251 reports. D.C. Code § 50–1731.07(b) says MPD gives DDOT a copy of each accident report, but no official page says DDOT gives individual reports to the public.

It is unclear whether DC drivers must currently file the Motor Vehicle Crash Report for PROPERTY DAMAGE ONLY form. The form PDF (created 2011) and MPD training material (approved 4/26/2023) describe it. But MPD's web page for the form now permanently redirects to DDOT's 'What To Do After A Non-Injury Crash?' page, which doesn't mention filing any form. DDOT's current checklist is marked for informational purposes only, DC DMV says not to report any crash to DMV, and the D.C. Code accident-report subchapter (§ 50–1301.10 et seq.) is repealed. The only submission details found are on a 2011 DDOT envelope PDF (DDOT - Safety Division Crash Records Box, PO Box 20164, Washington, DC 20077-7822; fax (703) 858-1358; www.ddot-hso.com/CrashForm), which I could not confirm as current. gaps.reason: No official page I read gives the exact amount of the Texas.gov surcharge or card processing fee. TxDOT calls it only a 'minimal surcharge' or 'minimal Texas.gov fee'. Finding the amount would mean starting a purchase, which was out of scope.

No official TxDOT page describes an in-person or walk-in way to get a crash report from TxDOT. The state pages describe only online purchase and the CR-91 mail form. Whether a local police department or sheriff offers walk-in copies varies by agency and was not researched agency by agency.

Official sources do not agree cleanly on mail. The live CRIS Purchase Help Center says you can still buy a copy by mailing the CR-91, and the CR-91 (Rev. 08/23) is still posted. TxDOT's main crash records page no longer mentions mail purchases of ordinary copies. It also says that since January 1, 2025 subpoena and affidavit requests are no longer accepted by mail, the CR-91 is no longer required for them, and 'all requests received by mail will be returned'. Confirm with the CRIS help desk before telling readers to mail an ordinary request.

The form number is inconsistent. TxDOT's crash records page, its CRASH page, its forms page and the CRIS Purchase User Guide call the officer's report the CR-3. The live CRIS Purchase Help Center, the purchase portal home page and the CRIS Request page call it the CR-4. I found no official explanation. Claims above keep each source's own form number.

The Texas Department of Public Safety page on crash records (https://www.dps.texas.gov/node/415) could not be opened: the connection was refused. So I include no DPS-specific facts, such as what DPS keeps for trooper-investigated crashes.

State sources show that TxDOT collects reports from every law enforcement agency. They also show that a governmental entity holding a report must release it under the same §550.065 rules and $6/$2 statutory fee. Each city police department's or sheriff's own request process, any extra fees, and any vendor portal it uses were not checked.

No current official source I read says plainly whether drivers must file their own written crash report with a state agency. It also gives no current form, deadline or threshold for one. TxDOT says it no longer keeps or provides the CR-2 and destroys any CR-2 submitted. The statute calls the old sections 550.061 and 601.004 'former'. The current law requires immediate notice to police for certain crashes (§550.026) and lets cities require reports by ordinance (§550.067). The CR-2's former deadline and threshold were not confirmed on a current official page.
No official source I read sets a time-based confidentiality period. Access depends on the requester's relationship to the crash under §550.065. Others get a redacted copy.

Official sources give only maximums, not a typical wait. These are: officers have 10 days to file, TxDOT may need up to 4 business days to process, a report can take up to 14 days to appear online, and mail can take up to 30 days.
